definitions.definition: The idea that every physical event has a physical cause, and nothing outside the physical world can affect it.
definitions.example: If you drop a glass, it breaks because of gravity and impact, not because a ghost pushed it.

definitions.definition: The belief that God exists completely on his own, not needing anything else to exist or be what he is.
definitions.example: A rock needs dirt and time to form, but God doesn't need anything to exist.

definitions.definition: Basic assumptions you accept before you can think or argue about anything else.
definitions.example: Before you can do a science experiment, you assume the world is real and your senses work.

definitions.definition: When a system uses itself to prove itself, like a dictionary that defines words using other words from the same dictionary.
definitions.example: Using the Bible to prove the Bible is true is a circular argument.

definitions.definition: A basic belief you choose to hold that everything else you believe depends on.
definitions.example: Deciding that science is the only way to know truth is a foundational commitment.

definitions.definition: The idea that you can't prove the future will be like the past using logic, because that would require assuming the future is like the past.
definitions.example: Just because the sun rose every day before doesn't prove it will rise tomorrow.

definitions.definition: The idea that something proves itself to be true without needing outside evidence.
definitions.example: The Bible claims to be God's word, and believers say they just know it's true because of how it feels inside.

definitions.definition: A statement accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for other reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.
definitions.first_appearance: First paragraph after 'Here's a question nobody wants to answer honestly.'

definitions.definition: A belief about the nature of reality or knowledge that you hold, often without being able to prove it.
definitions.example: Believing that only physical things exist is a philosophical commitment.
definitions.first_appearance: First paragraph after 'Here's a question nobody wants to answer honestly.'

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experience, not just theory.
definitions.example: A doctor's diagnosis is empirical if it's based on test results, not just guessing.
definitions.first_appearance: First paragraph after 'Here's a question nobody wants to answer honestly.'

definitions.definition: Able to be proven wrong by evidence or experiment.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan proves it wrong.
definitions.first_appearance: First paragraph after 'Here's a question nobody wants to answer honestly.'

definitions.definition: The assumption that the laws of nature are the same everywhere and at all times.
definitions.example: We assume gravity works the same on Earth and on Mars, even though we haven't tested it everywhere.

definitions.definition: Reasoning from specific examples to a general rule, like 'every crow I've seen is black, so all crows are black.'
definitions.example: If you see three white swans, you might induce that all swans are white.

definitions.definition: Mistaking something as belonging to a category it doesn't belong to, like asking 'what color is the number 7?'
definitions.example: Saying 'science disproved God' is a category error because science only studies physical things, not God.

definitions.definition: A big, shared way of thinking or model that guides how a field works.
definitions.example: Before Copernicus, the paradigm was that the sun goes around the Earth.
definitions.first_appearance: Paragraph starting 'We're going to walk through a graveyard of thirteen scientific paradigms.'
